Build a scientific ML workflow with a coding assistant, then test what changes
when you improve the data or the model. Read the explanations and saved results here;
expand **Show Python code** when you want the implementation.

## Get ready

1. Follow the [setup guide](SETUP_GUIDE.md), including Git, UV, VS Code and your coding-assistant options.
2. Download or clone the [complete repository](https://github.com/thiasyoung/2026-avs-ml-vibe-coding-workshop),
   then run [Check your installation](00_Test_Installation.ipynb) in its `.venv` kernel.
3. Open the [workshop roadmap](00_Workshop_Roadmap.ipynb). Each module's main path
   is **00 → 01 → 02**; acquisition is pre-work, and nested **Examples (optional)**
   are references rather than extra session steps.

::: {.callout-important title="IR module: download the dataset before the workshop"}
The repository does **not** include the native IR data. Open
[Workshop data v1 → Assets](https://github.com/thiasyoung/2026-avs-ml-vibe-coding-workshop/releases/tag/workshop-data-v1)
and download **ir_raw_checkpoint.parquet** (about 196 MB), not **Source code**.
Save it at `02_ir_functional_groups/outputs/nist_acquisition/ir_raw_checkpoint.parquet`
inside your cloned repository; create the folders if needed. This avoids repeating
the lengthy NIST scrape. See the [IR module guide](02_ir_functional_groups/README.md).
:::

## Three ways to practice

| Module | Your hands-on focus | Supplied starting point |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **01 · Boiling point** | Build and evaluate a SMILES-to-boiling-point pipeline. | Prepared molecular data, a ten-step prompting template and optional completed models. |
| **02 · IR functional groups** | Examine and clean spectra; compare preparation choices. | Native spectra, frozen holdouts and a fixed classifier. |
| **03 · HTEM process emulator** | Test algorithms, architectures and hyperparameters. | Prepared process/source/XY features, grouped splits and optional reference models. |

### 01 · Build a boiling-point pipeline

Review the ten-step template, then adapt the prompt in the workbook. Ask your
assistant to generate, execute and explain a pipeline. Chemprop, MoLFormer and
one-shot workflows are available as references, not prescribed solutions.

[Open the BP module](01_boiling_point/README.md){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

### 02 · Investigate IR data quality

Edit the carpentry workbook's starting plan and your hypothesis. Explore label
representation, units, signal types and spectral coverage, then produce the
uniform input files for notebook 02. Keep the classifier and holdouts fixed so
you can examine the effect of your preparation.

[Open the IR module](02_ir_functional_groups/README.md){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

### 03 · Experiment with an HTEM model

Use the supplied data preparation to predict thickness and conductivity at
individual substrate locations. Edit the model-workbook prompt to test an idea,
compare it with a baseline, and inspect both prediction errors and spatial maps.

[Open the HTEM module](03_htem_conductivity/README.md){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

## Use the workbooks

In IR and HTEM, **EDITABLE** includes the suggested workflow as well as blanks
for your hypothesis, plan, coding strategy, effort priorities and budget.
Only **FIXED input/output contracts** must stay unchanged. Copy the entire prompt
into your coding assistant; a prompt-only notebook does not run an AI by itself.

Download the whole repository rather than a single notebook: IR and HTEM use
shared helpers in `lib/`, and examples also rely on module data. Your workbooks
save separate outputs so you can keep completed references intact.

::: {.callout-note title="Read here; run in VS Code"}
These pages show the outputs last saved in the notebooks. They are not a live
Jupyter session, and publishing does not scrape data or train models. Some examples
need model downloads, training time or extra memory when rerun; see their module guides.
For a PDF, use your browser's **Print → Save as PDF**, expanding any code you want included.
:::
